after.description: The 1997-1999 3.0CL uses an automatic transmission specific to its V6 model family (the 2.2CL/2.3CL 4-cylinder variants do NOT share this transmission and are not affected). Owners and independent transmission shops widely report failures: slipping under load, not shifting out of 1st until warm, harsh shifts, and eventually total failure. Reports of repeat failures are common. NOTE: this transmission failure pattern is more severe and better documented on the 2nd-gen 3.2CL (2001-2003) than on the 1st-gen 3.0CL; the 1st-gen exhibits the same underlying weakness but at lower failure rates. A critical maintenance detail: this transmission has minimal internal filtration, and the filter is not serviceable without complete teardown. Owners who power-flush a slipping unit dislodge clutch debris and accelerate the failure rather than fix it.
after.solution: If symptoms appear, immediately switch to ONLY Acura/Honda ATF (never Dextron substitute) and start a regular drain-and-refill schedule at every engine oil change interval (6 months). Do NOT power-flush — this transmission has effectively no serviceable filter and pressurized flushing forces debris through tight passages. If slipping has already started, a transmission specialist (not a quick-lube) needs to drop the pan to check for clutch material in the fluid. Once debris is visible, only a rebuild fixes it ($2,500-3,500). Replacements/rebuilds may need a fresh torque converter — the original is a known weak point. Add an aftermarket transmission cooler at rebuild time; the factory cooling is undersized.

If you rebuild, add an aftermarket transmission cooler. Factory cooling is undersized and was a contributor to original failures.

after.description: All DA and DC Integras (and all Honda B-series transverse cars) use four hydraulic engine mounts: front, rear, passenger-side (the 'side mount'), and driver-side (the transmission mount). The rear and front mounts use a fluid-filled rubber bushing that wears out — typically the rear mount goes first by 100,000 miles, the passenger-side side mount second. Failure signs: clunk when shifting in or out of gear (especially on automatics), vibration at idle that disappears when you press the brake or shift to neutral, and a 'wheel hop' feeling under hard acceleration. Skipping motor mount replacement on a manual Integra accelerates wear on the half-shafts, transmission shift forks, and the trans itself, because the engine is moving around in the bay.
after.solution: Replace mounts one at a time as they fail, not all four preemptively (the front and side mounts can last 200k+). Diagnose by having a helper rev the engine in neutral while you look — a healthy mount holds the engine still; a dead one lets the engine rock 1-2 inches. Common pattern: rear mount + passenger-side mount are the first two to need replacement, and both are visible from above without lifting. Aftermarket options range from cheap rubber ($30 each) to Energy Suspension polyurethane ($60-100, transmits more vibration but lasts forever) to Innovative Mounts billet ($100-200, used for tracked cars). For a daily-driver Integra, OEM Honda rubber or Cardone is the right balance. Total cost replacing rear + side: $80-300 in parts, 2-3 hours of labor.

Diagnose before buying parts. Have a helper rev in neutral while you watch from the side — a healthy mount holds the engine still, a dead one lets it rock 1-2 inches. Replace only the dead ones.

Energy Suspension polyurethane mounts ($60-100) last forever but transmit much more vibration into the cabin. Great for track cars, terrible for daily-drivers — your steering wheel and shifter will buzz at idle.

after.description:
The CV joints are lubricated with grease and sealed inside rubber boots that hold the grease in and keep dirt out; over time the boots crack or tear, grease escapes and dirt enters the joint causing it to break down, and the joint develops excessive play in its bearings, producing a repetitive clicking sound when accelerating through a curve.
 
Clicking or popping noise when turning is the classic sign of a worn outer CV joint, most obvious during sharp low-speed turns like in a parking lot; vibrations while accelerating and dark heavy grease splattered on the inner edge of the tire are additional symptoms.
 Common on the B18A1-powered DA chassis where the outer boots crack with age and especially after donuts in reverse or hard cornering.
after.solution:
If the boot has just torn and no elements got into the joint, regreasing and rebooting can work — a $10 boot kit vs. a $60 replacement axle is the tradeoff.
 
Reman axles run around $50 each and boot kits about $25 — AutoZone and similar carry both for the 1992 Integra 1.8L DOHC.
 
Pack outer CV joint boot with molybdenum disulfide grease, lube the spider and inside bore of rollers, ensure rollers are aligned with marks made at disassembly and install with the high side of rollers facing outward.
 Use new boot clamps (low-profile metal bands included in kit). Most owners simply swap the full reman half-shaft for under $100/side — quicker than rebooting. Always replace the axle nut and use a new transaxle retaining ring.

communityRecommendations.content: Inspect both outer boots at every oil change — catching a tear early lets you reboot for $25 instead of replacing the axle.
DA Integras use a dynamic damper (weight) on the axle shaft — make sure any replacement half-shaft includes it or transfer the original.

after.description: The Integra's ignition system uses a discrete ignitor module (also called ignition control module, or ICM) mounted inside the distributor cap. The module triggers the coil and is a known failure point on 1990-2001 Integras — replacement units are stocked by most major parts retailers (Beck Arnley, Delphi, Standard Motor Products). Failure presents as a no-spark condition: engine cranks normally but will not start, or starts intermittently. Often happens after the engine reaches operating temperature, then the car will not restart until the module cools — though owners report the failure mode varies. NOTE: 1990-1993 Integras use the OBD-0 diagnostic system, which produces numeric flash codes (e.g. code 15 for ignition) rather than the OBD-II P-codes used from 1996+. The original Honda heat sink part #30121-PM5-A02 mentioned in some installation guides is now discontinued/out of production.
after.solution: Test the ignitor before replacing — a multimeter check at the coil primary terminals while cranking will confirm whether the module is sending pulse to the coil. If no pulse: replace. OEM Honda module $80-150, aftermarket (Beck Arnley, Delphi) $30-80. The module sits inside the distributor cap; replacement requires removing the cap and rotor, unscrewing 2 mounting screws, and transferring the heat sink if present (Civic/Integra units may require heat sink #30121-PM5-A02 for correct fitment). Inspect the inside of the distributor cap and rotor for moisture or corrosion while you're in there — a cracked cap allows water in and causes premature module failure on the replacement. Replace cap + rotor at the same time as a preventive measure.

citations.title: Acura Integra Igniters — PartsGeek (OEM + aftermarket catalog with fitment 1990-2001)
Acura Integra Ignition Control Module — AutoZone

communityRecommendations.content: Beck Arnley or Delphi ignitor — $30-80, works well for daily-driver use. OEM Honda ($80-150) is more durable if you're keeping the car long-term.
Replace the distributor cap and rotor at the same time. A cracked cap lets in moisture that fails the module again within months. Both parts are under $50 combined.
Test before replacing. Use a multimeter on the coil primary terminals while cranking — if the module is pulsing the coil, the no-start is somewhere else (often the main relay).

after.description:
The PGM-FI Main Relay is a critical electronic switch that sends power to the fuel pump and engine computer (ECU); when you turn the key it clicks on, allowing the pump to build pressure and the computer to manage the engine — without a working main relay the engine won't get fuel or the electronic commands it needs to run.
 
The main relay is a known weak point on DA-chassis Integras — over many years the solder joints inside the relay crack from heat and vibration, and the problem is often worse on hot days or after the car has been running, as heat causes the cracked joints to expand and lose connection.
 Symptoms include crank-but-no-start after the car sits in the sun, intermittent stalling, and the fuel pump failing to prime audibly when the key is turned to ON.
after.solution:
Replacing the main relay is one of the easiest repairs on the Integra; it is located under the driver's-side dash, near the hood release lever and to the right of the parking brake pedal — unbolt the mounting bracket (10mm), unplug the harness, and plug in the new relay.
 
Use a quality replacement — the DA-chassis OEM part number is typically 39400-PM6-003 (verify with your VIN at an Acura dealer or parts store, as several supersessions exist). Reputable aftermarket cross-references include Standard Motor Products RY-passenger-style relays, Beck/Arnley, and Denso. Expect to pay $25-$80 for the part and avoid the cheapest generic relays — reliability matters.
 
Resoldering the cracked joints on the existing relay's circuit board has been done successfully by many owners, but requires skill with a soldering iron and may not be permanent — a new aftermarket relay is the more reliable repair.

citations.title: 1993 Acura Integra Won't Start in Hot Weather — 2CarPros
1990 Acura Integra Trouble Starting the Car — 2CarPros

communityRecommendations.content: Carry a spare main relay in the glove box — they're small and a roadside swap can save a tow.
Diagnose first: turn key to ON and listen for the 2-second fuel pump prime. No prime + no audible relay click = main relay.

after.description:
The wheel bearings on the 1990-1993 Acura Integra (DA chassis, second generation) are critical parts located inside the wheel hub assembly — for the DA-generation Integra these are press-in style bearings pressed into the steering knuckle in the front and the hub/spindle in the rear, and they support the full weight of the car while it's in motion.
 
When a wheel bearing starts to go bad it usually gives warning signs; ignoring them can lead to serious problems including the wheel separating from the car, and the most common sign is a humming, rumbling, or grinding sound that gets louder with speed.
 
The hum is often hard to localize from inside the cabin — passengers in the back may each think it's on their side — but it typically lessens when steering loads the bad bearing's opposite side (e.g., turning right unloads the left side, so if noise decreases when turning right, the left bearing is likely the culprit).
after.solution:
This is an advanced DIY job. Some owners replace the rear as a complete pre-pressed hub assembly (commonly $80-$120 from aftermarket suppliers), which avoids press work; others source just the bearing/race and press it into the spindle/knuckle using a hydraulic shop press (or have a machine shop do it). Front bearings on the DA always require pressing into the knuckle.
 Quality replacement brands include SKF, Timken, FAG, Koyo and NSK (the latter two are often OEM suppliers to Honda).
 Rear bearings are a bit more expensive but easier to access than the fronts.
 Budget $40-$120 per bearing/assembly plus press/labor; total shop cost typically $200-$450 per corner.

citations.title: rear end making a loud humming noise — Team Integra
DIY Rear Wheel Bearing Replacement — Team Integra
Acura Integra Bad Wheel Bearing Noise Diagnosis — Drivetrain Resource

communityRecommendations.content: Diagnose by steering side-to-side at highway speed: if the hum lessens when steering right, the bad bearing is on the left (unloaded) side, and vice versa.
For the rear, you can often buy a complete pre-assembled hub/bearing unit for roughly $80-$120, which avoids needing access to a hydraulic press.
Stick with Koyo or NSK bearings — they were the original Honda OEM suppliers and outlast most cheap aftermarket kits.

after.description:
The Honda BAXA/MAXA 4-speed automatic in the Integra is notoriously sensitive to fluid condition and shift-solenoid contamination. Solenoid A/B failure causes flashing D4 light, harsh or missed 2-3/3-4 shifts, loss of power in D4/D3, and sometimes speedometer drop-out. 
Integra often faces delayed or missed shifts and manual downshifting difficulties in automatic transmissions. Shifting problems in the 1998 Integra's automatic transmission can stem from a clogged transmission filter or screen restricting fluid flow. This causes poor hydraulic pressure, leading to missed 4th gear shifts and failure to downshift.
 
While driving, the D4 suddenly lost almost all power, wouldn't shift, and the speedometer stopped working. Codes returned were Automatic Transaxle FI A circuit failure and ELD error.
after.solution:
Drain-and-fill with Honda ATF-Z1/DW-1 (NEVER use generic Dexron — it will destroy the clutches). 
The transmission fluid in the Integra 4AT's are supposed to be changed every 3 years/36,000 mi. It can cook and wear out just like the oil in your engine.
 Pull codes with a Honda jumper or scan tool; the lock-up and shift solenoids are external, three-bolt parts accessible from the engine bay and often just need cleaning. 
A screwed up lock-up solenoid will give you a general CEL #70 (Automatic Transaxle); the solenoid is totally accessible from the engine bay and costs less than $200 to replace. It's held in place by three bolts.

communityRecommendations.content: Use only Honda ATF-Z1 or DW-1. Generic ATF causes shift flare and premature failure.
Pull the specific solenoid code before condemning the transmission — a $150 solenoid often fixes it.

after.description:
The TEC/Hitachi internal-coil distributor on third-generation Integras is a chronic failure point. Heat from the internal ignition coil degrades the coil, igniter (ICM), and bearings, causing intermittent stalling at operating temperature, hot-restart problems, and dead no-starts. 
The 1996 Acura Integra has the most overall complaints, with the most-reported problem being distributor failure. This issue can cause difficulty starting the car, stalling, and misfiring.
 
The car has been in the shop because the driver was driving and it just shut off with no warning or light. Come to find out it was the distributor so they changed it.
after.solution:
Pull DTCs first — codes P1381 (cylinder position sensor) and Code 22 commonly originate inside the distributor. 
P1381 is the cylinder position sensor code, located inside the distributor.
 Replace the complete OEM distributor assembly (avoid cheap aftermarket — many fail within months). OBD1 (94-95) and OBD2 (96-99) distributors are not interchangeable. 
It is worth noting that the distributor plugs are different for each obd generation. So the obd1, and obd2 have different harness plugs.
 Budget $250-550 for a quality unit installed.

after.description:
The electrical contact block on the steering-column ignition switch develops pitted contacts. The car will crank and start, but as soon as the key returns from START to RUN the contact fails and the engine dies. Sometimes the car will run if the key is held partially toward START. 
Driving home and the 95 Acura Integra 4 door GSR died on the highway. If trying to start the car, it would start then die as the key was released. Holding the key close to III kept the engine on. The ignition harness switching mechanism contact point was pitted.
after.solution:
Replace the ignition switch electrical portion (not the cylinder/lock) — it unbolts from the back of the steering column lock housing with two screws. OEM Honda part is the most reliable choice. 
The issue is starting the car and it dies as soon as you let go of the key. After research, it became obvious it was an ignition switch issue.
 Check the under-hood main fuse and the ignition fuses before condemning the switch. Budget $50-150 for parts and 1 hour labor.

after.description:
The long bolts that pass through the rear lower control arm inner bushings corrode to the steel sleeve inside the bushing. Any attempt to remove them for alignment, bushing, or shock work results in a sheared bolt and a destroyed bushing sleeve. This is a near-universal complaint in rust-belt cars. 
Owners had to cut the ears that go around the LCA off the strut because the bolts rust to the inside of the bushing.
 
LCA bolts break ALL the time.
after.solution:
Soak bolts with penetrating fluid (PB Blaster/Kroil) for days before attempting removal; heat the bushing sleeve with a torch. If the bolt shears, the only fix is to cut the bushing out and drill/punch the remaining sleeve from the subframe ear. 
When you are down there and replacing rusted bolts, if they are rusted on bad enough you might have to break the welded nut they go into on the front side of the subframe and trailing arms. You can get matching sized nuts and washers.
 Replace with a new vehicle-specific rear lower-control-arm bolt kit. Match the exact seized location and OE dimensions before installation; several rear-LCA fasteners are used on this chassis.

citations.title: Lower Control Arm Bolt Replacement — Team Integra
Rear Lower control arm bolt? — Team Integra

communityRecommendations.content: Spray penetrating oil into the bushing sleeve through both ends a week before the job.
Use proper-grade OEM bolts — hardware-store bolts are not always the correct grade for this safety-critical joint.

after.description:
All B18 engines in the 1994-2001 Integra (DC2/DB7) are interference-design. If the timing belt snaps (or jumps teeth from a seized tensioner or water pump), pistons strike open valves. The belt should be replaced every 90,000 miles along with the water pump, tensioner, and seals.
The timing belt in the DOHC Honda engine keeps the engine running and valvetrain events on time. Because the 1.8 liter B18 engine is an interference engine, failure of the timing belt usually means pistons have hit valves. This can lead to lack of cylinder compression at the bare minimum. At worst the valve may become stuck or destroy the piston.
after.solution:
Replace the complete timing belt kit: belt, tensioner, tensioner spring, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance shaft belt where applicable.
Non-VTEC LS (B18B1) timing belt part numbers are 14400-P7J-004 or 14400-PR4-A01, paired with the 19-tooth water pump 19200-P75-003 / 19200-PT5-000 / 19200-PT5-003. The VTEC GSR (B18C1) uses timing belt 14400-P72-004 / 14400-P72-014 paired with a 22-tooth water pump.
Do NOT mix LS and GSR water pumps — the tooth counts differ (19T vs 22T) and the belts are different lengths.
Professional cost for preventive replacement: approximately $350-600. Post-failure repair (valve job / head rebuild) can reach $2,000-3,000+.

citations.title: How To Change a B18B Timing Belt — My Pro Street
How To Change Your B18C1 DOHC VTEC Timing Belt — My Pro Street

communityRecommendations.content: Use a Japanese-made kit (Aisin water pump, Mitsuboshi or Gates belt) — avoid no-name kits.
Replace at 90k miles or 5 years even if the belt looks fine; tensioner bearings can seize without warning. Honda's published interval is 90,000-100,000 miles or 5 years under normal conditions.

after.description:
The VTEC oil pressure switch screwed into the VTEC solenoid assembly on B18C engines fails or leaks, triggering CEL with OBD1 Code 22 or OBD2 P1259. Symptoms include VTEC not engaging at high RPM and a hard rev-limiter drop. 
Owner had a 99 GSR with CEL constantly on and code 22 (VTEC Oil Pressure Switch). Even after replacing it with a new one and swapping the VTEC solenoid, the problem occurred after going into VTEC and letting off, mostly around 60-90mph.
 
Error code 22 corresponds to the front valve timing oil pressure switch, which is the VTEC oil pressure switch.
after.solution:
Verify oil level and condition first — 
if the code is still present after checking, make sure there is plenty of oil and then reset the ECU
. The switch is the green-plug sensor on top of the VTEC solenoid; replace with OEM Honda part. 
Replace the switch. It's the green plug located on the vtec solenoid.
 If the code returns after replacement, install a mechanical oil pressure gauge — 
a worn oil pump or internal leak can cause low pressure that triggers the code; an oil pressure gauge will confirm
. Switch is ~$70 OEM.

after.description: The Integra turbo engines experience significant heat soak during spirited driving in ambient temperatures above 85 degrees F, causing noticeable power loss after sustained high-RPM driving. The intercooler efficiency drops as the engine bay temperature rises, and the ECU pulls timing aggressively to protect the engine.
after.solution: Allow 2-3 minutes of gentle driving between spirited runs to cool the intake charge. Ensure the intercooler fins are clean and unobstructed by debris. Aftermarket intercooler upgrades significantly reduce heat soak on the 1.5T. The Type S 2.0T is less affected due to its larger factory intercooler but still benefits from airflow improvements. The 2.0T Type S application begins with model year 2024; 2023 applications are 1.5T only. Match the intercooler to the engine and trim.

communityRecommendations.content: On the 1.5T, an aftermarket front-mount intercooler (like the PRL Motorsports unit) drops intake temps by 30-40 degrees and virtually eliminates heat soak. It is the single best performance modification for the Integra.

after.description: The Sumitomo ALB (Anti-Lock Brake) system on G2 Legends uses a high-pressure hydraulic pump and nitrogen-charged accumulator in the right front engine bay. The pump motor brushes wear out causing the pump to run more than 2 minutes continuously (ABS Code 1), and the accumulator loses nitrogen charge over time. Result is ABS light on, pulsing pedal at low speed, or noisy continuous pump operation after engine start.
after.solution: Rebuild the pump motor (clean commutator, replace brushes — DIY for $30) or replace pump/accumulator assembly. Verify brake fluid is at MAX line first since low fluid triggers identical symptoms.

after.description: The 3.2L C32A/C32A1 V6 (1991-1995 Acura Legend) uses an open-deck block with a graphite (not multi-layer steel) head gasket. Engine vibration concentrated at the rear of the block wears through the gasket between the unsupported cylinder tops and the deck surface, almost always failing at cylinders #3 and #6 (cylinder #6 is the most failure-prone). Coolant enters the cylinders causing white exhaust smoke, coolant loss, misfires, and eventually hydrolock. The Type-II C32A1 (1993-1995 coupe LS/L, 1994-1995 GS sedan), especially with the 6-speed manual, sees accelerated failure due to higher loads.
after.solution: Replace both head gaskets with a verified 1991–1995 C32A/C32A1 set, resurface the heads, and torque to specification. Confirm gasket construction and engine compatibility before installation. A long-term fix sometimes pursued in the enthusiast community is swapping to a later C-series engine (e.g., C35A from a 1996+ RL) which uses improved gasket technology.

after.description: The radiator/condenser fan control unit, located under the passenger floor carpet, suffers cracked solder joints on its circuit board from heat cycling. Symptoms include rad fans not coming on (causing overheating at idle), fans running at full speed at every startup, A/C clutch engaging with the switch off, or random fan/AC behavior. Honda/Acura Service News B98-05-00 (May 1998, 'Fan Control Unit Causes Warm A/C') documents diagnosis; the defect is widely reported on 1991-1992 units and some 1993 units.
after.solution: Pull the fan control unit from under the passenger carpet and reflow the cracked solder joints (10+ joints typically affected) with a soldering iron, or replace the unit. DIY repair is well documented and effectively free.

after.description: The PGM-FI main relay (under the dash, driver's side near the fuse box) controls power to the ECU and fuel pump. PCB solder joints develop hairline cracks from vibration and heat cycling. On hot days (90F+) or after a hot soak in the sun, the cracked joints open and the car cranks but will not start until it cools 5-15 minutes. Same failure mode as virtually every 1988-2000 Honda/Acura.
after.solution: Pull the relay, open the case, reflow all solder joints with a fine-tip iron (free fix). Or replace with OEM Omron unit ($50-100). Aftermarket relays often fail again quickly.

after.description: The PS high-pressure hose deteriorates internally from age, heat, and the constant 1,000+ psi pressure. Common at 100k+ miles on all G2 Legends.
after.solution: Replace the high-pressure hose with OEM Honda part and flush the entire PS system with fresh Honda PSF (NOT generic ATF or universal PSF — Honda systems specifically require Honda PSF). Replace return hose at the same time.

after.description: Each sunroof corner has a small drain tube routing through the A-pillars (front) and down through the quarter panels to outlets behind the rear wheel wells (rear). The tubes clog with debris or split with age (rubber becomes brittle), allowing rainwater to overflow into the cabin. Front clogs flood the driver/passenger footwell carpet; rear clogs flood the trunk spare tire well.
after.solution: Open the sunroof and locate the four drain holes at the corners of the tray. Clear with thin trimmer line or controlled low-pressure air, then flush with water. Excess air pressure can blow a drain tube off its fitting. If tubes are split, headliner removal is required to replace them.

after.description: Both valve cover gaskets and the six rubber spark-plug tube seals harden and shrink with age, leaking oil down the engine and into the spark plug wells. Oil pooling in the plug wells causes misfires and damaged coil/wire boots. The driver-side bank is significantly harder to access on the G2 Legend's longitudinal V6 — bolts near the automatic transmission fluid dipstick make DIY replacement a multi-hour job on that side. Common at 80k+ miles on any G2 Legend.
after.solution: Replace both valve cover gaskets, all six spark plug tube seals, and the half-moon seals at the same time. Use OEM Honda gaskets — aftermarket gaskets often leak again within 30k miles.

after.description: First-generation MDX models with the J35 V6 are prone to timing belt tensioner bearing failure and simultaneous water pump leaks when the timing belt service is neglected past 105,000 miles. The hydraulic tensioner loses pressure, allowing the belt to skip teeth and potentially bend valves on this interference engine.
after.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, water pump, and all idler pulleys as a complete kit at 105,000 miles or 7 years, whichever comes first. Use genuine Honda/Acura components or the verified AISIN kit matched to the year split: TKH-001 for 2001–2002 and TKH-002 for 2003–2006. Never reuse the old tensioner even if it appears functional. This is a critical interference engine — a broken belt destroys the valves.

after.description: Like every C-series V6 Honda used in the 1990s and 2000s (Legend, NSX, CL, TL, RL all share the family), the RL's 3.5L C35A V6 has a distributor mounted at the back of the head and driven directly off the camshaft. Inside the distributor housing, an oil seal isolates the cam-driven shaft from the cap/rotor/electrical assembly above. By 100,000 miles the seal hardens, oil pressure forces engine oil past the shaft, and the cap fills with oil. Result: misfires (typically P0300 random plus individual cylinder codes P0301-P0306 since this is a V6), rough idle, hesitation. RepairPal explicitly lists distributor O-rings as one of the most common Acura RL oil leak points. The figure-8 oil cooler seal and oil filter housing gasket are the other two common leaks on this engine — diagnose carefully before assuming distributor. The C35A engine remained in the first-gen RL through the entire 1996-2004 production run, so this issue affects all years.
after.solution: There is no replaceable seal inside the distributor — the seal is between the rotating shaft and the bearing inside the cast housing. The only fix is replacing the whole distributor assembly. OEM Honda runs $400-700; Cardone remanufactured runs $150-250. While the distributor is out, also replace the distributor cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and you're already at the parts. Inspect the cap and rotor on the old unit for oil contamination to confirm distributor was the source. If you also see leaks elsewhere (figure-8 cooler seal, oil filter housing), address those at the same time — they share access path. Total job: 2-3 hours independent shop.

Don't assume distributor without inspection. RepairPal also lists the oil cooler 'figure-8' O-ring and oil filter housing gasket as common RL leaks. Pull the cap and check for oil before buying the distributor.

after.description: The first-gen RL's 3.5L C35A V6 is part of the Honda C-series V6 family, which is widely documented as interference design (valves and pistons share rotational space, separated only by timing belt synchronization). The published timing belt interval is 105,000 miles or 84 months per the maintenance schedule. The hydraulic timing belt tensioner on this generation has been reported by independent shops as a known failure point: the internal oil seal leaks, the tensioner loses pressure, the belt can jump a tooth or two, and valves can hit pistons. Multiple sources caution that aftermarket tensioners have a worse failure rate than OEM Honda or Aisin — pay for the OEM-equivalent kit. Note: belt replacement intervals are sometimes quoted as shorter (90,000 mi) by independent shops as a conservative buffer, but the manufacturer-published interval per Acura is 105k/84 months for this engine family.
after.solution: Replace the timing belt, tensioner, water pump, idler pulley, and required front seals as one service. Match the kit to the 1996–1999 C35A application and verify the tensioner manufacturer before installation; no current AISIN TKH-022 application was verified. Never perform a belt-only service on this interference engine.

after.description: The 2nd-gen RL's Super Handling All-Wheel Drive uses a torque transfer unit (TTU) at the transaxle output plus a rear differential containing electromagnetic clutch packs for variable side-to-side torque distribution. With age and fluid breakdown, both can develop a low-speed grinding or moaning noise — most often the rear unit's electromagnetic clutches when SH-AWD fluid is contaminated or below spec.
after.solution: Drain and refill the rear differential with Honda Dual Pump II fluid — do NOT use conventional gear oil. If noise persists after fluid change, the rear differential unit needs rebuilding with new clutch packs. Replace the electromagnetic actuators if they are not engaging properly. Regular fluid changes every 30,000 miles prevent premature clutch pack wear.

after.description: The SLX is a rebadged Isuzu Trooper, and inherits the same drivetrain failures that plague the Trooper. The rear differential develops a high-pitched whine, primarily under load at highway speed, caused by ring-and-pinion wear from imperfect gear mesh. Once the whine starts it progressively worsens; if ignored, the gears can strip. Separately, the Borg-Warner transfer case used in 1998-1999 SLX/Trooper has documented seal-leak and bearing-wear failures. CRITICAL FLUID NOTE: do not assume any specific fluid spec without checking your service manual — early sources circulated incorrect fluid specifications for the Borg-Warner transfer cases used in these vehicles. Always verify the correct fluid by manufacturer documentation or a Borg-Warner technical lookup before topping off — using the wrong fluid is a known cause of accelerated failure.
after.solution: REAR DIFF: If whine is noticed early, change the gear oil to fresh 80W-90 GL-5 and run a friction modifier. This will not stop existing wear but can slow it. Once whine is pronounced, the only durable fix is a remanufactured rear axle assembly ($800-1,400) or a rebuild of the existing ring and pinion ($1,200-2,000 at a specialist). TRANSFER CASE: Verify the manufacturer-spec fluid is being used — DO NOT default to motor oil or ATF without confirming. Check fluid level every oil change. If the case is whining or has external leaks, source the correct Borg-Warner rebuild kit by part number from your vehicle's exact model year + transmission combination — multiple BW transfer case variants were used across SLX/Trooper years and the parts are NOT interchangeable.

BW4422 transfer case rebuild kit (BK4422) — covers seals, bearings, chain on the 1998-2002 SLX/Trooper/VehiCROSS transfer case. $300-500 in parts.
Catch rear diff whine early — fresh GL-5 80W-90 with friction modifier won't reverse wear but can buy 10-20k miles of grace before a rebuild is mandatory.

after.description: Many TL owners report front brake judder, steering wheel shake, and pulsation under moderate braking, often traced to uneven rotor deposits or rotor distortion. The heavier curb weight of the TL, combined with driving style and pad/rotor material, appears to make the front brakes prone to repeat issues. Complaints and forum reports show some owners needing multiple resurfacing or replacement jobs over the life of the car.
after.solution: Inspect rotor thickness variation, pad condition, caliper slide movement, and wheel torque. Replace or machine rotors if within spec, install quality pads, and service caliper hardware to prevent uneven pad contact. Proper wheel lug torque and a careful pad bedding procedure help reduce recurrence.

after.description: The Vigor's 2.5L 20-valve SOHC inline-5 (G25A1) is an unusual engine — Acura's only 5-cylinder, mounted longitudinally to fit between the Integra and Legend slots. Like every other Honda V6/I5 of the era, it's an interference engine: timing belt failure means valves crash into pistons. Honda's interval is 90,000 miles or 6 years. The original belts on 1992-1994 Vigors have all aged out. The same hydraulic tensioner used on the C-series V6s is on this engine and has the same wear-out pattern. The water pump weep is the most common warning sign — coolant pooling at the base of the timing cover means the seal is gone and you need to do the full job.
after.solution: Replace the timing belt, belt tensioner/adjuster, water pump, idler, front seals, and accessory belts as one service. No complete current AISIN kit was verified for the G25A1, so source the exact components separately and use an OEM Honda or independently verified OEM-quality tensioner/adjuster. Avoid unverified no-name timing components.
